messages.subject: Interpreting covariate influence if interaction is not significant?
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting covariate influence if interaction is not significant?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have been setting up Multi-Species-Occupancy Models for 2 Species, using the occumulti() function. I have allowed interaction to vary with covariates.

Some of my models showed non-significant p-values of the interaction-term, but the selected covariate still showed significant p-values... Also some of the plots gave a "significant-like" look, when plotting the interaction against the selected covariate. Nonetheless my intuition tells me, in cases when the intercept of the interaction is not significant, to not  interpret covariate effects.

Am I right or am I maybe missing something important here?

Thanks in advance

Maresa

Hello,

I am using occumulti() to explore species pairwise co-occurrence patterns. Here, detection is a function of a survey specific categorical covariate with two levels (A and B). In the species detection histories, the first 14 occasions are using level A and the remaining 8 are using level B. For species 1, only levels A applies (the last 8 occasions have NAs in the detection history) and for the other species, both levels apply. Now, I want to fix the detection probability for level B for species 1 to zero. Otherwise, it is automatically converting B detections to NA for the other species also.  What would be the argument to fix this parameter to zero?

Thanking you for your help.

Divyajyoti

messages.subject: Re: Interpreting covariate influence if interaction is not significant?
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting covariate influence if interaction is not significant?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Maresa,

The value of the interaction term is the combined values of the intercept + covariate effect. So I don't think it would be correct to look only at the value of the intercept, it also matters what's happening with the covariate. As you say at some values of the covariate, if the associated slope has a large (in an absolute sense) value, the total interaction term may be different from 0 at that value. Looking at the plots can help with this.

Consider the extreme situation where the interaction term is modeled as a function of a single categorical covariate with two levels (say, habitat types A and B). The intercept by itself will represent  the interaction term in habitat type A and the slope the additional effect of B. If the model estimates the value of the intercept at 0 and the effect of B at say 3 (with some small SE 0.2), it is clear that species are more likely to occur at the same sites in habitat B (total interaction term 3) but not in A (0). We wouldn't want to say there was no interaction in either habitat just because the intercept was 0.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi Divyajyoti,

In order for a sampling occasion to be usable by the model both species must have been sampled during that period. That's why an NA for any species on an occasion converts the rest of the samples to NA as well. So unfortunately there isn't a way to incorporate the final 8 sampling periods (and their associated covariates) into the model if species 1 was never sampled during that period.

It *may* be possible to incorporate the extra data for species 2 somehow with a custom model in e.g. BUGS, but I doubt it.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am new to using 'unmarked' but am trying to run an occupancy model looking at occupancy of warty pigs (indirect signs) in grid squares across a National Park. Due to the data I was given and limited resources, temporal replicates of the species surveys weren't able to be completed. Multiple transects (2-5) were conducted within each grid square (site), with each transect split by several checkpoints and counted as spatial replicates. These checkpoints were in theory supposed to be equal distances apart, but as with all field surveys due to topography/obstacles meant that this was not the case. I was given the GPS tracking of each transect and used ArcGIS to get their distances. As a result, each repeat in my data frame has a corresponding transect distance in another column (i.e. R1, R2, R3, R4... ; R1_dist, R2_dist, R3_dist, R4_dist...).

This comes to my problem of incorporating this into the model: accounting for differences in transect/repeat length, in addition to the fact that each site has a different number of replicates (so there are a number of NA values within the data frame). I can't use total distance of all the transects as a covariate as each transect is responsible for a different 1/0 presence/absence value within the data frame and differences in distance will affect detection. From what I understand these are survey specific detection covariates that I am trying to incorporate.

I have had a deep dive into google and there doesn't seem to be much out there concerning this, since most survey designs have replicates of the same length. I realise that the data collection may seem quite messy and inconsistent, but I am just involved in the data analysis and occupancy calculations.

Thank you in advance for any help given.
Georgina

Hi Georgina,

It seems to me that these transects lengths are an observation-level covariate, which you would provide to the obsCovs argument when you create your unmarkedFrameOccu (see ?unmarkedFrameOccu for the help page). It's OK if you have missing observations (NA) in either the actual observations or an observation covariate.

Ken

I think I'm a bit confused about your study design, which may be the reason for the problems with the obs covs.The hierarchy is sites --> transects --> checkpoints, right? What do you consider to be your sampling unit here (i.e., where you are ultimately recording a 0 or a 1), transects, or checkpoints within transects?

If your unit of sampling is checkpoints nested within transects nested within sites, unmarked doesn't directly support such a 3-layer sampling structure. You could pool detections and obs covs (such as distance) across checkpoints within transects, leaving you with just sites and transects. Another potential approach is to make transects your "sites", and checkpoints within transects your sampling occasions, and then include a random effect of (original) site on occupancy.

Ken

OK thanks. Your data frame looks correct to me. I think the issue is with the specification of the obsCovs. What you should do for the obsCovs is extract from the data frame columns R1_dist to R11_dist and turn them into a separate matrix called e.g. "dist" with dimensions nsites x 11. Then in your call to unmarkedFrameOccu, you would pass this in the form of a named list to obsCovs, e.g.

umf <- unmarkedFrame(y = y, siteCovs=[DATAFRAME WITHOUT R1-R11], obsCovs=list(dist = dist))

If you had other observation covariates you would make matrices out of them also and include them in the list, e.g. obsCovs = list(dist = dist, cov2 = cov2)
Then in your model your formula use the name from your list, something like ~dist~[SITE COVS]. This will line up the appropriate distance values with the appropriate observations.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tiago,

fewer observations don't necessarily mean that you are less likely to get a fitting model in a GoF test like this --- in fact quite the contrary may be true: with less data you have less power to detect patterns that don't look right under your model and are thus less likely to obtain a significant GoF test.

The test output yields at least a little bit of insight into WHERE your model does not fit (at least with respect to time, but not with respect to sites). That is, where the differences between your observed data, and what the model says the data should look like, are greatest.

For the wet season, the total chi-square for the actual data is about 2100, while for a fitting model one would expect a value of about 580 (that's the median of the bootstrap distribution). The value for the full data set is obtained by summing the values of the test statistic over all the years. Thus, under a fitting model one would expect annual values of about 580 / 11 = 53. For the observed data, the chi-square contributions from years 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 look about OK, but for the other years there is strong lack of fit, mostly so in years 4, 7, 8 and 11. Perhaps you can now imagine some process that might have lead to something "special" in these seasons ? And perhaps you can then add a covariate that expresses that effect and in this way improve the fit of your model ?

Finally, you could also adopt what some might say is a dirty little trick, but what is widely done in the analysis of count data: claim that the lack of fit detected is just "overdispersion", or unstructured noise, rather than the result of a structural breakdown of the model somewhere. Then, you can adjust your SEs and AIC scores by the estimated value of c-hat. However, there are some rules of thumb out there about how large the value of c-hat may be so that you can still take this approach without blushing too much  .... I think the usual upper value is about 3. So, even if you want to take that approach, it might be good to tinker a bit with your model to get a better fit in the first hand.

Best regards  --- Marc

> Dear Tiago,
>
> fewer observations don't necessarily mean that you are less likely to get a fitting model in a GoF test like this --- in fact quite the contrary may be true: with less data you have less power to detect patterns that don't look right under your model and are thus less likely to obtain a significant GoF test.
>
> The test output yields at least a little bit of insight into WHERE your model does not fit (at least with respect to time, but not with respect to sites). That is, where the differences between your observed data, and what the model says the data should look like, are greatest.
>
> For the wet season, the total chi-square for the actual data is about 2100, while for a fitting model one would expect a value of about 580 (that's the median of the bootstrap distribution). The value for the full data set is obtained by summing the values of the test statistic over all the years. Thus, under a fitting model one would expect annual values of about 580 / 11 = 53. For the observed data, the chi-square contributions from years 1, 2, 5, 6 and 9 look about OK, but for the other years there is strong lack of fit, mostly so in years 4, 7, 8 and 11. Perhaps you can now imagine some process that might have lead to something "special" in these seasons ? And perhaps you can then add a covariate that expresses that effect and in this way improve the fit of your model ?
>
> Finally, you could also adopt what some might say is a dirty little trick, but what is widely done in the analysis of count data: claim that the lack of fit detected is just "overdispersion", or unstructured noise, rather than the result of a structural breakdown of the model somewhere. Then, you can adjust your SEs and AIC scores by the estimated value of c-hat. However, there are some rules of thumb out there about how large the value of c-hat may be so that you can still take this approach without blushing too much  .... I think the usual upper value is about 3. So, even if you want to take that approach, it might be good to tinker a bit with your model to get a better fit in the first hand.
>
> Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tiago,

yes, I think the number of occasions or their spacing should be taken account of automatically in an occupancy model.

A common approach to OD is to claim that its causes are benign (i.e., simple noise) and then to account for the resulting added uncertainty by making SEs and CIs larger. Specifically, by multiplying the SEs by the square root of the estimate of c-hat and computing CIs using these 'stretched' versions of SE. As for the AIC, there is an overdispersion-corrected version called QAIC. These methods should be implementable for dynocc models using the AICcmodavg R package.

Best regards  ---- Marc

Hello everyone,

messages.body_plain:
You probably want to look at "multistate occupancy models".  Typically "multistate" is applied to the "occupancy" part of the model such that rather than just presence or absence of lizards you might have "present and breeding", "present and not breeding", and "not present".  But in your case the multiple categories seem to be just in the detection part:  (1) observations that clearly identify occupancy, (2) observations that are just consistent with occupancy, and (3) no indication of occupancy.  If the probability of (2) is much higher in occupied sites than in unoccupied sites, the use of such lower-level detection observations can reduce the variability in the estimators of the occupancy probabilities.

Creating the model and finding the maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters is not unsurmountable but it would be a whole lot easier if some software already existed.  If no software exists, then a first step might be to set up the model and estimation code for individual years.

Jim

messages.body_plain:
The siteCovs should be a data frame with dimensions N x P where N is the number of sites and P is the number of site-level covariates.

The obsCovs should either be (1) a data frame with dimensions N*J x P2 where N is the number of sites, J is the number of occasions, and P2 is the number of obs-level covariates; or (2) a named list of matrices each with dimensions NxJ, one matrix per observation covariate.

It sounds like you want to use a site-level covariate (i.e., one measurement per site) as an observation-level covariate. If that's the case, just include it siteCovs. You can still use it in detection formulas.

Ken
